title: Meet Divya Panicker, Kochi oceanographer decoding India’s hidden whale choir, building underwater network to protect marine giants
content: Kochi: For centuries, pygmy blue whales, some nearly 24 metres long, have been singing a haunting three-note melody off India's southwest coast. Their low-frequency calls travel hundreds of nautical miles across the ocean, remaining beyond the range of human hearing. In October 2019, oceanographer Divya Panicker finally heard them. Inside a quiet island home in Lakshadweep, the Kochi-born researcher sat with headphones on, listening to audio retrieved from a recorder anchored 25 m on a reef beneath the ocean surface. Outside, roosters crowed in the morning. Through her headphones came something far more extraordinary: the deep pulse of a pygmy blue whale, the first such recording from Indian waters. She jumped up and down in disbelief before texting her mentor. It was amazing to sit on the island and suddenly realise it is right here off the reef, and you're hearing these songs. The cool thing is they have been singing here for years, it's just that human ears can't hear those frequencies without equipment, Panciker recalls while speaking to Onmanorama. Recently named in the inaugural TIME100 Next India 2026 list for her pioneering marine-mammal research, Panicker has spent nearly 15 years making sense of the ocean's hidden soundscape. What began as a fascination with wildlife has evolved into a conservation mission spanning India's waters. She is now on a mission to establish an underwater hydrophone and audio-recorder network to monitor whales in Lakshadweep. Growing up in Kochi's Vyttila, she rarely visited the beach. Television wildlife documentaries, however, introduced her to the natural world. After a BSc in Zoology from Stella Maris College, Chennai, and a Master's in Wildlife Management in the UK, an internship in Scotland brought her into the world of marine mammals. She went on to study humpback dolphins navigating the busy boat traffic inside Kochi harbour. A defining experience came in 2013, when her mentor, renowned wildlife biologist Dr Ajith Kumar, took her on a cyclone-battered research voyage across the Bay of Bengal. He had cautioned her that whale research was hardly glamorous, but encouraged her nonetheless, opening doors into a field that would eventually take her to Lakshadweep. The underwater world she studies is largely invisible. Beyond the first few dozen metres, sunlight fades, leaving whales and dolphins dependent on sound to navigate, communicate and find mates. Male blue whales produce repetitive, low-frequency songs capable of travelling nearly 1,000 kilometres through deep water. Panicker calls them true champions at long-distance relationships. According to Panicker, unlike blue whale populations elsewhere that migrate thousands of kilometres towards polar waters to feed, pygmy blue whales in the northern Indian Ocean appear to remain in the region throughout the year. Seasonal monsoon winds churn up nutrient-rich deep waters, encouraging microscopic plants to flourish and supporting dense populations of krill, the tiny shrimp-like creatures on which the whales feed. Their importance extends well beyond their size. Whales act as 'ocean farmers', feeding in deeper waters and releasing nutrient-rich waste near the surface, helping fertilise phytoplankton at the foundation of marine food chains. Imagine an elusive giant, bigger than any other giant ever to have lived on this planet, able to speak across ocean basins, helping phytoplankton grow, and eating some of the tiniest animals. It's remarkable that these gentle souls share the same waters with us, she says. Panicker's research has now moved beyond individual discoveries. In 2025, she launched an ambitious five-year project to establish underwater listening stations across five Lakshadweep islands. Every six months, she dives to depths of 35 m alongside local divers to retrieve the recorders, download terabytes of audio and redeploy them...
